title: What is known about 1RB0LF_1RC0RB_0RD1LE_0LE0RA_1LC1LA_0LD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LF_1RC0RB_0RD1LE_0LE0RA_1LC1LA_0LD---.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project; an outside Rocq proof has since shown that it never halts when started on a blank tape. The head sweeps across the whole tape, which is written in four-cell words. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it never halts. Busycoq pull request 87 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-17) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer has not yet reviewed it. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

What this repository found on its own. Lean proves the exact way a halt would happen (1 1 E>1), that the other way into A is harmless, and how the sweeps cross the four-cell words; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 1011 steps. How the list of counters evolves was not worked out here. The proof reads the tape differently, as a crystal and a long word that both grow every cycle (see the explainer).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: How a halt comes about
claims.text: F reading 1 is the only halt. F is entered only from A reading 1 (enter_F), which writes 0 and steps left, so the machine halts exactly at 1 A>1. A is entered from D reading 1 and from E reading 1 (enter_A); the D way is harmless (via_D_safe), so a halt needs 1 1 E>1 (halt_E), reached from 1 1 1 C>1 or 1 1 1 D>0.

claims.title: The way in through D is harmless
claims.text: A is entered from D reading 1, moving right; D writes 0 there, so when A reads 1 and steps back left, F reads that 0 and goes on. For every surrounding tape.

claims.title: Crossing the words
claims.text: For every n and every surrounding tape, moving right: D turns (1000)^n into (0110)^n, A turns (0001)^n into (1100)^n, C turns (0100)^n into (0011)^n, B turns (0010)^n into (1001)^n and erases 1^n. Moving left: E carries a 0 across (0001)^n, D across (0010)^n, and E and C fill (0 1)^n and (1 0)^n into 1s.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator (tools/c/tm.h) runs 1011 steps from blank tape without a halt; the visited tape then spans 457,337 cells, 207,592 of them 1.

claims.title: E never reads 1 next to 1 1
claims.text: In the first 2·109 steps E reads 1 about 169 million times; the two cells on its left are 0 0, 1 0 or 0 1, never 1 1.

claims.title: A list of counters
claims.text: When the head reaches the left end the tape reads C>0 (1000)^k ... or E>0 (0001)^k ... followed by a long list of runs (0100)^a1 (0111)^b1 (0100)^a2 (0111)^b2 ... (or the same in the shifted words 0001 / 1101), with values such as 13, 25, 58, 46, 25, 34, ... The same values reappear in the same order sweep after sweep; the list changes only next to the left counter and in an active zone near the right end.

claims.title: Growth shape
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.562). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.487).

claims.title: Size of the tape description (family screen)
claims.text: At the 8 records between 2.6·10<sup>8</sup> and 1.6·10<sup>10</sup> steps (first new leftmost or rightmost cell after each threshold 10<sup>6</sup>·4^k) the tape has 31,354 to 195,526 visited cells and compresses to 1,033 to 4,135 level-2 tokens (repeats of a word of at most 40 cells, then repeats of groups of such tokens).

claims.title: Proposed family: F06, block-list counters
claims.text: With repeats of single words only, the number of pieces is proportional to the tape (18,641 level-1 tokens for 195,502 cells at 1.6·1010 steps). Most of them are one block of long period: [(0100)^13 (0111)^10 (0100)^4 (0111)^13 (0100)^10 (0111)^4]^N with N = 69 at 4.1·109 steps and N = 363 at 1.6·1010 (left-end records; a period of 216 cells). With such groups counted once, the left-end records have 2,772 and 2,817 level-2 tokens at 4.1·109 and 1.6·1010 steps and the right-end records 4,033 and 4,135: the rest of the tape hardly grows over a factor of 4 in steps. Right of the block the tape is a frozen list of runs of growing lengths (10, 37, 16, 28, 19, 34, … up to 202) and then a list of units (1110)^a (1000)^3 111 (0100)^b (0111)^3 01 000 with a and b between 3 and 42. The table is that of 1RB0RA_0RC1LD_0LD0RE_1LB1LE_1RA0LF_0LC--- with the states renamed (related.json), from another start; that machine shows the same period-216 word with other counts. The two runs are different and nothing is claimed about one from the other. A list of units that changes slowly while a periodic block grows behind it is read here as a list of counters: F06. The round rule was not found here; the outside proof gives one (one cycle adds two copies of a 66-cell pattern and 312 letters to a word).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape? (this repository’s own ledger)
claims.text: Not decided by the results on this page alone. It is decided outside: busycoq pull request 87 proves that it never halts (see the verdict). Before the proof, this ledger said that a proof would describe how a sweep pair acts on the list of counters (where values are consumed and new ones are written) and show that three 1s in a row never meet E or C or D in the halting way. Window CTL up to 7 cells and n-gram CPS (widths up to 9, see the README for the larger runs) fail.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RA_0RC1LD_0LD0RE_1LB1LE_1RA0LF_0LC--- up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: It never halts. Its tape is written in four-cell words. Left of the head lie a crystal, one 66-cell pattern repeated many times, and a long word of four-cell letters, with fixed pieces around them. Each cycle adds two copies of the pattern and 312 letters, and the proof shows that the cycle repeats for ever.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
The only way it could stop; the other way in is harmless. The proof shows it never comes up.
169 million times E read 1, never next to 1 1.

sections.heading: A crystal and a long word that grow every cycle
html: The proof is busycoq pull request 87 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind. We compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1, and it uses no axioms. This machine has the table of 1RB0RA_0RC1LD_0LD0RE_1LB1LE_1RA0LF_0LC--- with the states renamed, started in another state; pull request 85 proves that one in the same way, and the two proofs find the same crystal and the same growth per cycle. With a reduction already in busycoq it also settles the equivalent machine 1RB1RD_0LC1RA_0RA0LD_1LE0RF_1LB0LE_0RC---.

The shape of the tape. The proof watches the machine in state B at the right end of the tape, on a blank cell, with everything else to its left. Write P for one fixed pattern of 66 cells and Pc for P written c times: this is the crystal. Let w be any list of bits, written on the tape in four-cell letters: 0001 for a 0 and 0010 for a 1. Read from right to left, starting at the head, the tape is a short fixed piece, the crystal Pc, a long fixed piece of about 18,000 cells (the proof stores it compactly as a list of letters), the word w, and a last fixed piece that includes 16 copies of 0011. The proof calls this family of tapes decode w c hub_start: one tape for every word w and every count c.

One cycle. From any tape of the family the head sweeps back and forth across the crystal and the word many times and comes back to a tape of the same family. By then c has become c + 2. The word has 42 new letters at its end nearer the head and 270 new letters at its far end, the same letters every cycle, and the old letters in between are kept (the proof also allows them to come back all flipped). The key point is that the head treats every letter of w alike. The rules for crossing the word work letter by letter for any word, so the machine never needs to know what w says, and one computation covers every w and every c at once. A cycle ends on a tape of the family, so it can be repeated for ever, and the machine never halts.

The numbers. The proof follows the machine with a fast simulator that crosses a whole copy of P, a whole run of a four-cell word, or the whole word w in one step. After one step of the machine, it takes 3,844,054 such steps to reach the first tape of the family; on the way it forms the crystal once and tidies the tape into the family's shape 27 times, across stretches of more than 95,000 pieces. One cycle is 29,113 steps and one more tidying. The 270 letters added at the far end fill 1,080 cells, five periods of 216 cells, which fits the block of period 216 that this repository saw growing in its runs.

What is proved and what is computed. Eleven short pieces of the machine's run are checked step by step. From them the proof derives, by induction, rules for crossing any word w, any run of a four-cell word and any number of copies of P, in both directions. A theorem then says that every step of the fast simulator is a true piece of the machine's run, whatever w and c are. The tidying only rewrites the same tape in the family's terms (it adds copies of P to the count c and joins lists of letters), which is plain algebra on lists. The computer checks the rest with Coq's vm_compute: that the simulator started from the blank tape reaches the family, and that one cycle started from the family returns to it.

sections.heading: A list of numbers in four-cell words
html: Stop the simulator each time the head reaches a fresh cell at the left end. The tape reads

A counter of words 1000 sits at the left end, then a long list of runs of the words 0100 and 0111. The same numbers come back in the same order sweep after sweep: the sweeps rewrite each word (into 0001 / 1101 and back) but keep the counts. The list changes only next to the left counter and in a zone near the right end.

sections.heading: The one way to halt
html: The only missing transition is F reading 1. F is entered only from A reading 1, which writes 0 and steps left; A is entered from D reading 1 (then F reads the 0 that D just wrote, which is safe) or from E reading 1, moving left. So the machine stops exactly when
1 1 E>1   →   1 A>1 1   →   F>1 0 1   halt
This is proved in Lean (lean/Halt.lean). The tape is sparse in 1s where E works, and in 169 million visits the two cells left of E were never both 1.
The outside proof shows that this pattern never comes up: the run stays in a family of tapes on which every cycle returns (first section).

sections.heading: Which family it belongs to
html: The 22 machines of family F09 (“bouncers over lists of counters, not yet classified”) were screened in one way. The machine runs from blank tape for 2·1010 steps; each time the tape reaches a new cell after a threshold, the tape is compressed twice: first repeats of one word, then repeats of groups of words. If the tape is a few growing blocks and a bounded rest, the number of level-2 tokens stays bounded while the tape grows. Everything in this section is observed in one run. None of it is proved.
Proposed family: F06, block-list counters (a periodic block of long period, a frozen list of growing runs and a list of counters at the right).

With repeats of single words only, the number of pieces is proportional to the tape (18,641 level-1 tokens for 195,502 cells at 1.6·1010 steps). Most of them are one block of long period: [(0100)^13 (0111)^10 (0100)^4 (0111)^13 (0100)^10 (0111)^4]^N with N = 69 at 4.1·109 steps and N = 363 at 1.6·1010 (left-end records; a period of 216 cells). With such groups counted once, the left-end records have 2,772 and 2,817 level-2 tokens at 4.1·109 and 1.6·1010 steps and the right-end records 4,033 and 4,135: the rest of the tape hardly grows over a factor of 4 in steps.

Right of the block the tape is a frozen list of runs of growing lengths (10, 37, 16, 28, 19, 34, … up to 202) and then a list of units (1110)^a (1000)^3 111 (0100)^b (0111)^3 01 000 with a and b between 3 and 42. The table is that of 1RB0RA_0RC1LD_0LD0RE_1LB1LE_1RA0LF_0LC--- with the states renamed (related.json), from another start; that machine shows the same period-216 word with other counts. The two runs are different and nothing is claimed about one from the other.

A list of units that changes slowly while a periodic block grows behind it is read here as a list of counters: F06. The round rule was not found here; the outside proof gives one (one cycle adds two copies of a 66-cell pattern and 312 letters to a word).
The proof (first section) reads this tape with fewer pieces: one crystal of a 66-cell pattern and one long word, both growing every cycle.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.562). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.487).
After 109 steps the tape spans 65,047 cells (43,045 left of the start, 3,324 right), with a density of 1s of 0.443.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the cycle described in the proof section.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: Bouncer whose tape is a long list of counters written as alternating runs of the words 0100 and 0111, kept from sweep to sweep and changed only near the ends; it halts only if E reads 1 with 1 1 on its left. Decided outside: busycoq PR 87 proves in Rocq that it never halts (compiled here).
family: two-sided bouncer, a list of counters in the words 0100 / 0111
